_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: The ba’al happikin and the ikkel: as [the mishna] explains, and it explains the ikkel first. Anyone who “surrounds his soles”: when he sits and brings the soles of his feet together, his knees do not knock against each other, since they bend outward.
rashi:a1.2: A protuberance emerging from his thumb: a round piece of flesh, like a knob [pika], protruding from his thumb.
rashi:a1.3: His heel emerges behind him: as the Gemara explains, his shin stands in the middle of his foot, so that half the foot is in front and half behind.
rashi:a1.4: Wide like a goose’s: they are flat like a goose’s, and their length is no greater than their width.
rashi:a2.1: Until the joint: the middle joint.
rashi:a2.2: Below the joint: that is, toward the nail, where they are all joined; and he cut it so that they are separated: he is fit.
rashi:a2.4: If it contains a bone, he is disqualified: since he cut it off, he is now missing a limb that he had. And if not, he is fit, since it counts as no more than a wart.
rashi:a3.1: Six and six, twenty-four: the Gemara explains, in connection with the verse, why it uses these terms; the mishna simply uses the verse’s wording.
rashi:a4.1: Gemara. The kishan: that is, one who knocks his ankles together.
rashi:a4.2: And the ikkel and the kilban: that is, a protuberance emerging from his thumb.
rashi:a4.3: We read: ba’al happikin and the shufnar. [Rashi reads happikin, with a pe, where the translation has hakkippin.]
rashi:a4.4: Many pads [kesatot harbeh]: his ankle bone, which is called (Rashi adds an Old French gloss), is very large. [The translation renders kesatot as “protuberances.”]
rashi:a5.1: Tereifa [rendered “flat” in the translation]: (Rashi adds an Old French gloss).
rashi:a7.1: “Above” in the baraita is the same as “below” in the mishna.
rashi:a8.1: And when it is counted along the back of the hand: it is counted with the other fingers, standing in their row. That is the case the mishna teaches, since then it counts as a limb.
rashi:a9.1: If it had a bone and no nail: [the baraita] states the greater novelty: even though it has no nail, it counts as a limb if it is counted along the back of the hand.
rashi:a9.2: It imparts impurity by contact, by carrying and in a tent: for example, where it has a little flesh, but not an olive’s bulk. For if it had an olive’s bulk of flesh, it would impart impurity in a tent even if it were not counted [with the fingers] or had no bone, since an olive’s bulk of a corpse imparts impurity in a tent. And if it had no flesh at all, then even if it were counted, so that it counts as a limb, it would not impart impurity in a tent, since bones impart impurity in a tent only as a majority of the skeleton, a majority of the number of bones, or a quarter-kav. But now that there is a little flesh, it imparts impurity even without an olive’s bulk, since it is counted along the back of the hand and counts as a limb. For so we say in Tractate Niddah, chapter Yotze Dofen (Niddah 43b): limbs have no minimum size; even less than an olive’s bulk of an animal carcass, or less than an olive’s bulk of a corpse [imparts impurity].
rashi:a9.3: And it is included in the count of 125: if it has no flesh, it is included in the count of 125, which is a majority of the number of a corpse’s limbs, since a corpse has 248 limbs, and a majority of the number of a corpse’s [limbs] imparts impurity in a tent. And when it is counted: if it does not stand in the row of the fingers, it does not count as a limb, since it has no nail.
rashi:a10.2: But it does not impart impurity in a tent: this is where it is not counted, as [Rabbi Yoḥanan] explains, so that it has two shortcomings: it has no nail and it is not counted. But if it has a nail, it imparts impurity [in a tent] even though it is not counted; and so we learned in the chapter Ba Siman (Niddah 49a).
rashi:a11.1: Like statements of prophecy: prophets need not give a reason for their prophecy, since people listen to them without a reason; so too, they gave no reason for their statement.
rashi:a15.1: And even though there is not a quarter-kav among them, they are impure: in a tent. It is taught in connection with [Tractate] Oholot.
rashi:a15.2: Since this is a majority of the height of an adult: a majority of the height of a grown person whose limbs are not dwarfed. For two shins and one thigh are a majority of the height of the body without the head, since the head is not counted in the structure of a corpse, in the baraita of Oholot that teaches: What is its structure? The shins and the thighs, the body and the spine. Another version: we read “since a majority of its structure is in height [ba-godel],” and that is the wording of the Tosefta. Ba-godel: in height.
rashi:a16.1: Is the tanna coming to teach us a number? Asked in surprise: since there are 248 limbs, it is obvious that 125 are a majority.
rashi:a16.2: Lacking, with only 200: one who was created lacking two fingers on each hand and each foot, that is, eight fingers; and each finger has six bones, as is explained in Tractate Oholot. So 48 are missing from the fingers, and only 200 remain. And extra, with 281: for example, a woman who was created with four extra fingers on her hands and feet. Four extra fingers are 24 more bones, and a woman has two hinges, two doors and a key, as we say below. That makes 29 extra limbs; add them to 248 and you have 277. As for the remaining four, I do not know how they come about, for each finger certainly has only six bones in all and nothing more [literally, “neither root nor branch”], and so it is explained in Oholot.
rashi:a16.3: All of them are included in the count of 125: all these extras count as limbs and are included in the count of 125. And we learn from this that even though 125 is not a majority of this one’s limbs, since he had 281, nevertheless 125 counts as a majority. And with the one who is lacking, too: even though [101] would be a majority of his, nevertheless only 125 counts as a majority.
rashi:a17.1: Hinges [tzirin]: (Rashi adds an Old French gloss).
rashi:a19.1: For Rabbi Akiva: with the key, there would be 253, which is difficult in light of Rabbi Yishmael’s students, who found only 252.
rashi:a19.2: Since it is small: the key dissolved because of the boiling.
rashi:a20.1: And all of them: all these extra [limbs] in a woman do not impart impurity in a tent as a limb on its own with a little flesh on it.
rashi:a21.1: Hinges of flesh: this is an answer. Without a bone it does not count as a limb.
rashi:b2.1: Six of his and six of his foot: he had extras on one hand and on one foot, and not on both.
rashi:b3.1: Like you, may mamzerim and Gibeonites decrease from Israel: may all the mamzerim in Israel be like you, so that they are recognizable as coming from unfit seed, and [people] will not cling to them [in marriage].
rashi:b4.1: Left-handed in the foot: when he walks he lifts the left foot first, which is not the way of people. One who is left-handed in the hand is disqualified, as it is written: “And he shall dip his finger,” and wherever “finger” and “priest” are stated, it means only the right (Zevaḥim 24a). And one who is left-footed [is disqualified] too, since it is written “to stand to serve,” in the manner of all standing, which rests mainly on the right.
rashi:b4.2: As one Sage holds that a weakness began: in his right [hand].
rashi:b5.1: Mishna. The kushi, the giḥor, the lavkan and the kipe’aḥ: explained in the Gemara.
rashi:b5.2: And those with pure marks: for example, a sappaḥat [a type of skin mark]. For impure marks need not be stated, since [such a person] would be liable to karet even for entering the Temple courtyard.
rashi:b5.3: Taltulin: like pieces of flesh that protrude and hang from them. [Rashi’s text reads taltulin where the printed mishna reads dildulin.]
rashi:b6.1: Gemara. Sumka [red]: (Rashi adds an Old French gloss).
rashi:b6.2: Lukiyani: they were white lambs. People customarily call a red one gohya.
rashi:b7.1: Long, emaciated [shemita], ugly: he is tall and thin, not broad in proportion to his height; and because he is thin he cannot bear his height, so he stoops and looks as if his vertebrae have slipped [shemutot].
rashi:b8.2: Tafuaḥ [rendered “dark”]: black as a pot. Similarly, at the end of Tractate Shabbat (157a): “and they stopped up the skylight with a tefiaḥ [an earthenware vessel].”
rashi:b9.2: He profanes the service: as it is written: “Drink no wine nor strong drink” (Leviticus 10:9), and after it: “And that you may put difference between the holy and the common.”
rashi:b9.3: Together with the blemishes: it should have been counted with the full blemishes, yet it is taught with the blemishes that disqualify because one is not equal among the seed of Aaron, about which we said at the start of our chapter that they do not profane the service.
rashi:b10.1: And not in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda: who gives other intoxicants the status of wine, which profanes the service. As it says in Tractate Keritot (13b): for wine, [the penalty is] death, and for other intoxicants, a prohibition; and we derive it from “strong drink, do not drink,” after which it is written, “and that you may put difference between the holy and the common.” Evidently, according to Rabbi Yehuda other intoxicants profane the service.
rashi:b10.2: As it is taught: one who ate pressed figs of Ke’ila: which grow in that place and intoxicate like wine.
rashi:b10.3: Honey: (Rashi adds an Old French gloss), [that is,] water and honey boiled together. He is liable to lashes: we establish this as Rabbi Yehuda’s view in the chapter Amru Lo in Keritot (ibid.), where it says that for other intoxicants there is a prohibition from “do not drink.” Since other intoxicants are written [in the verse], they profane the service, for it is written “between the holy and the common.” And our mishna, which does not count them with those that profane the service, is not in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda.
rashi:b11.1: Mishna. Itself and its offspring: it is disqualified as an offering, since it is “lacking time” [and may not be offered until the next day].
rashi:b12.1: And one who marries women by a transgression: a divorcée or a ḥalutza.
rashi:b15.1: Gemara. Ada amra: this is to say.
rashi:b15.2: In males: the father with the son or daughter.
rashi:b16.1: He vows and serves: even though he has not yet divorced her, he is permitted to serve once he has vowed that she will not benefit from him, nor he from her.
rashi:b17.1: He must delineate: one who comes to have his vow dissolved must specify what he vowed about; and when [the Sage] hears that he vowed because she is unfit for him, he will not dissolve his vow.
rashi:b19.1: A vow taken in public: this is a dispute in Tractate Gittin (46a), in the chapter HaSholeaḥ Get, concerning one who divorces his wife because of a vow.
tosafot:a4.1: A ba’al happikin, who has many pads [kesatot]: the Kuntres [Rashi] explained that his ankle bone, called (Tosafot repeat Rashi’s Old French gloss), is large. The Arukh explained that his foot is high, with much flesh toward the front of the foot and at the heel, and its middle is like a dome. The word kesatot [cushions] suggests the Arukh’s interpretation, that it speaks of flesh and not of bone, like the passage in Bereshit Rabba that says of a person, whose excretory place is covered by the buttocks, that he has kesatot, which is not so for an animal.
tosafot:a11.1: They rendered their statements like statements of prophecy, whichever way you look at it: since [the Gemara] raises a difficulty with it, this implies that “statements of prophecy” was not said in praise. But in the first chapter of Bava Batra (12a) it implies that it is said in the sense of importance, since it cites there [the teaching] that even though prophecy was taken from the prophets [it was not taken from the Sages]. I have explained this at the end of the chapter Keitzad Me’abberin (Eruvin 60b).
tosafot:b10.1: Through other intoxicating agents, and not in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda: in what is taught at the end of the first chapter of Zevaḥim (14b), that a non-priest, an acute mourner, a drunk and a blemished priest disqualify [the blood] in receiving, carrying and sprinkling, one may wonder why it mentions “a drunk”; it should have said “those who drank wine” and “those with overgrown hair.” The sage Rabbi Ḥayyim Kohen, may his soul rest in Eden, says that it speaks of other intoxicating agents and follows Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that [such a priest] profanes the service, just as we establish the drunk here as one [made drunk] by other intoxicating agents.
tosafot:b18.1: This works out well according to the one who says one must delineate: this is a dispute between Rav Naḥman and Rav Pappa in the chapter HaSholeaḥ (Gittin 35b). It seems that the halakha follows Rav Pappa, that one must delineate, since he is the later authority. And even according to the texts there that read Rav Sheshet in place of Rav Pappa, the halakha does not follow Rav Naḥman [whose rulings are usually followed in monetary law], since that question was not raised as a monetary matter, about a widow who comes to collect her marriage contract, but as a matter of prohibition, as is implied there, where it says: “And if you say one must delineate, sometimes he will cut his words short.” And Rav Huna too, who is greater in wisdom and in years, holds there that one must delineate.
tosafot:b19.1: In brief: Rashi located the dispute in Gittin 46a, where Rabbi Yehuda rules that one who divorced his wife because of a vow the public knew of may not remarry her, because of the impropriety [of a vow that cannot be released], while if the public did not know of it he may remarry her, since he is not concerned about a mishap. Tosafot ask how we know that the Rabbis there disagree and hold that a public vow can be nullified; perhaps they differ from Rabbi Yehuda only about the concern for a mishap. They answer that in that sugya the Talmud also takes it as obvious that the Rabbis hold it can be nullified, since the Rabbis ask whether the oath to the Gibeonites was binding at all. One might argue that since the Rabbis do not distinguish between a known and an unknown vow, the public vow must be nullifiable; but they also do not distinguish a vow taken on the consent of the public, which everyone agrees cannot be nullified. Tosafot answer that neither the Rabbis nor Rabbi Yehuda discussed the consent of the public at all, so their silence there proves nothing; but where Rabbi Yehuda did distinguish a vow made in public, the Rabbis would have had to say so had they agreed it cannot be nullified. Further, a vow on the consent of the public can sometimes be released, with the consent of those people or for a mitzva, so the mishna could not state flatly that the husband may remarry; whereas a vow in public, on this view, has no nullification at all, even for a mitzva, as the Gibeonite oath shows, which was for a mitzva. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
tosafot:b19.2: That we administer the vow on the consent of the public: one may ask from the beginning of the chapter HaSholeaḥ (Gittin 35b), about the widow, where Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel instituted that she vows to the orphans whatever they wish. Rav Huna says there: they taught this only when she has not remarried, but if she has remarried they do not administer the vow to her, since her husband can annul it for her even if she vowed in public. But why not? Let them still administer the vow on the consent of the public, which cannot be nullified, as Ameimar says here [on 46a]. One may explain that with regard to a wife’s vows there is no difference between “in public” and “on the consent of the public”: since according to Rav Huna her husband can annul a vow made in public, the same is true of one made on the consent of the public. And when [the Gemara] there challenges Rav Huna, “But let us be concerned that perhaps she will go to a Sage and he will release it,” and answers, “He holds that one must delineate the vow,” it could have answered that they administer it on the consent of the public, but it did not need to. Alternatively, Rav Huna does not hold like Ameimar: Ameimar’s statement, “even according to the one who says a vow taken in public…,” does not refer to the dispute of the Amoraim Rav Huna and Rav Naḥman at the beginning of HaSholeaḥ, but to the dispute of Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis at the end of HaSholeaḥ (Gittin 46a).
gershom:a1.1: Anyone who surrounds his soles: his soles are wide and round, so that when he brings his feet close together, his knees cannot knock against each other.
gershom:a2.1: A protuberance emerging from his thumbs: like an extra finger.
gershom:a3.1: His heel emerges behind him: it protrudes far behind him, as the Gemara explains: for example, his shin seems to come out of the middle of his foot.
gershom:a4.1: And the kilban: it has not been explained to us. [Some explain the kilban as one who throws his leg backward when he walks.]
gershom:a5.1: Happikin and the shufnar: many pads, like many ankles.
gershom:a6.1: Do not say flat: very thin, and not split between the toes but round like a goose’s; rather, once it is flat, even if it is split, he is disqualified.
gershom:a7.1: Attached until the joint: if the fingers are attached from the palm up to the middle joint of the fingers, he is fit; and if attached below the joint and he cut the attachment, he is fit.
gershom:a8.1: “Above the joint” said in the Gemara is the same as “below the joint” that we say in the mishna. Or [the baraita] includes all of these from “or.”
gershom:a9.1: [And when it is counted] along the back of the hand: it stands in the row of the fingers.
gershom:a10.1: And it is included in the count of 125: limbs, which is a majority of the number of the 248 limbs a person has.
gershom:a11.1: Our great rabbi: Rabbi [Yehuda HaNasi. Rashi identifies him as Rav].
gershom:a12.1: They rendered their statements like statements of prophecy: no one knows how to explain the reason why it imparts impurity by contact and carrying but not in a tent.
gershom:a13.1: They touched upon it because of a bone the size of a barley grain: a bone the size of a barley grain imparts impurity by contact and carrying and not in a tent; so too this one.
gershom:a14.1: Rav Pappa says: since it is not counted, by right it should not impart impurity even by contact and carrying; but it is a decree that one that is not counted imparts impurity because of one that is counted.
gershom:a15.1: If so: let them decree that one that is not counted imparts impurity in a tent because of one that is counted.
gershom:a16.1: They made a distinction with it: that it does not impart impurity in a tent, so that teruma and consecrated items will not be burned because of its impurity.
gershom:a17.1: Even though there is not a quarter: a quarter-kav of bones among them, they impart impurity in a tent.
gershom:a18.1: Two shins and one thigh: since this is a majority of a person’s structure in height.
gershom:a19.1: Lacking: a person lacking, who has only 200 limbs, for example, one who is missing two fingers from each hand and each foot; each finger has six bones up to the arm, so he is missing 48 limbs.
gershom:a20.1: And extra, who has 281: this one has 33 extra limbs, and these are they: he has four extra fingers on his hands and feet, which have 24 limbs; and for each set of six bones in a finger there is one corresponding bone in the arm, making 28 extras.
gershom:a21.1: And two hinges, two doors and a key: and that makes 281 limbs.
gershom:a22.1: All of them are included in the count of 125: even these extras are included in the reckoning of 125, for with the extra and the lacking alike we do not follow the majority of their own limbs but the majority of the limbs of ordinary people, which is 125.
gershom:a23.1: The [incident of] Rabbi Yishmael’s students is difficult for Rabbi Akiva: they found only four limbs more in a person, while for Rabbi Akiva, who adds a key, there are five limbs more.
gershom:a24.1: Perhaps since it is small: that bone of the key dissolved when they boiled it.
gershom:a25.1: And all of them: these five extras do not impart impurity in a tent.
gershom:a26.1: Hinges of flesh: and there are no bones in them.
gershom:a27.1: So too it is reasonable: that there are no bones in the hinges [of a man], for if you do not say so…
gershom:b1.1: I would say six of his: one [hand], and six of his foot: one [foot].
gershom:b2.1: Is that a proof? He did not say to him “may there increase [those] like you” as praise. Rather, he said to him: like you, may extra fingers increase among the mamzerim and Gibeonites in Israel, so that they are recognizable and decrease, as Israel will keep away from marrying them.
gershom:b3.1: One Sage holds: Rabbi, who disqualifies him [holds that] a weakness began in his right hand, since its strength is no greater than the left’s, and that is a blemish.
gershom:b5.1: Be’arikha shamuta sanya: long and thin, with a face that juts far outward, and unpleasant to look at; this is a blemish.
gershom:b6.1: Bohak: excessively white, which is a [skin] mark.
gershom:b7.1: Tefiaḥ: an earthenware vessel, black. [On the drunk:] it should have been counted with the blemishes, since all those in the mishna are not blemishes but are forbidden only because one is not equal among the seed of Aaron. A drunk profanes the service, as is explained in Tractate Zevaḥim.
gershom:b8.1: Through other intoxicants: for according to Rabbi Yehuda [the penalty is] death, and according to the Rabbis, a prohibition; their dispute is in the Sifra. [A note by the printed edition’s editor adds here: this is also the view of the Rambam, that a priest drunk from other intoxicants who served would be flogged; yet Keritot 13b implies that according to the Rabbis and Rabbi Elazar there is not even a prohibition; see the Kesef Mishneh on chapter 1 of Hilkhot Bi’at HaMikdash, and the matter requires further study.] [Rabbeinu Gershom then glosses the mishna’s word:] Dildulin: a wart [taltul].
gershom:b9.1: Itself and its offspring: [a father and son who are] priests are fit to serve together; and likewise a priest who is a tereifa, or was born by caesarean section, is fit for the service.
gershom:b10.1: One who marries women by a transgression: for example, a widow to a High Priest, or a ḥalutza to an ordinary priest. He is disqualified until he vows not to benefit from them, so that he will divorce them.
gershom:b11.1: He vows not to benefit and performs his service on the altar, and when he comes down from his service he divorces; he need not divorce before he serves.
gershom:b12.1: But let us be concerned: [and so] not permit him to serve before he divorces, lest after he has performed the service he go to a Sage and ask about his vow, and the Sage release it, and it turns out that he does not divorce.
gershom:b13.1: He holds: the one who says “he vows and serves” holds that one must specify what one vowed; and since he explains to the Sage that he vowed in order to divorce his wife who is unfit for him, the Sage will not release that vow.
gershom:b14.1: That we administer the vow: to him before the public, that he will divorce her, and a Sage cannot nullify it.
